paragraphs.heading: Speed against distance
paragraphs.text: A rotation curve, also called a velocity curve, is a graph for a disc galaxy. It shows how fast the visible stars or gas are orbiting, plotted against how far they sit from the galaxy's centre. The two sides of a spiral galaxy usually do not match, so astronomers average them to draw one curve.

paragraphs.heading: What gravity predicts
paragraphs.text: If Newton's laws of motion are correct, it seems to follow that most of a galaxy's mass should sit in the central bulge. Then stars and gas farther out in the disc should orbit more and more slowly the farther they are from the middle. Real curves do not do this. Outside the bulge they stay flat: the orbital speed is nearly the same at every distance.

paragraphs.heading: A mass that light misses
paragraphs.text: So the measured curves clash with gravity applied to the visible matter. The amount of mass you would guess from a galaxy's light is far too small to account for the speeds. The main proposed answer is dark matter: a large amount of matter spread through the galaxy beyond the bulge that gives off much less light for its mass than the bulge does. Other ideas exist, the best known being modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND), which changes the laws of gravity.

paragraphs.heading: Early measurements
paragraphs.text: Vesto Slipher took the first related measurements in 1914, looking at the Andromeda galaxy. Stars on one side of its bulge were coming toward us at around 320 km/s, faster than those on the other side at about 280 km/s, which hinted the disc was spinning. In 1957 Henk van de Hulst and colleagues used a new 25-meter radio telescope at Dwingeloo to measure an extended curve for M31 that agrees well with modern data. A companion paper by Maarten Schmidt showed the curve fit a flattened spread of mass reaching farther than the light.

paragraphs.heading: Rubin and Ford
paragraphs.text: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Vera Rubin worked with a new, sensitive spectrograph that measured the velocity curves of edge-on spiral galaxies more accurately than ever. In 1975 she and Kent Ford announced that most stars in spiral galaxies orbit at about the same speed. That meant a galaxy's mass keeps growing roughly in step with radius, well past where most of its stars are. Either Newtonian gravity does not apply everywhere, or more than half of a galaxy's mass lies in a dim halo. Doubted at first, her results have been confirmed in the decades since.

paragraphs.heading: A ruler from rotation
paragraphs.text: Rotation also links to brightness through the Tully–Fisher relation. For spiral galaxies, the rotation speed is tied to how luminous the galaxy is overall. Measure one and you can read off the other from the Tully–Fisher diagram. So how fast a galaxy turns is connected to how much visible mass it has.
